title: Never Disparaging (Kern ch. 19)
hookLine: a bodhisattva bows to everyone: I don't despise you, you will become a Buddha; they throw stones, he bows from further off

cards: A monk walks up to a stranger on the road, bows low, and says: I don't despise you. You will become a Buddha. The stranger stares, then gets angry.
Who asked for this man's opinion? Up comes a stick, or a handful of stones. The monk steps back out of range and says it again, louder, from further off.
That is very nearly the whole of chapter nineteen in Kern's numbering, and the chapter says it went on like that for a long time.

teach.b: First, the monk. The Buddha tells of a time long ago, after an ancient Buddha had passed away, when arrogant monks held sway. A bodhisattva monk did not spend his days reciting scriptures.

Whenever he saw anyone, monk or nun, layman or laywoman, he went up, bowed, and said: I do not despise you. You are walking the bodhisattva path, and you will become Buddhas. Second, why it angered people.
Some heard an insult wrapped in a compliment. Who was he to make predictions about them? They shouted at him and struck at him with sticks and clods of earth.

teach.h: HE STEPS BACK AND SAYS IT AGAIN.
teach.b: He stepped out of reach and called the same words back from a distance. He didn't change his line, and he didn't strike back. That is how he got his name.
In the Chinese translation it is Never Disparaging. Some readers hear two things at once in the Sanskrit name, Sadaparibhuta: the one who never despised, and the one who was always despised.

Fourth, who he turned out to be. Near the end of his life, the chapter says, he heard the Lotus Sutra, his senses were made clear, just as yesterday described, and his life was lengthened so he could teach it.
Those who had mocked him came to listen.
Then the Buddha tells the assembly: that monk was me.
And some of the people who once threw the stones are sitting here now.

how: In Tendai and Nichiren Buddhism, Never Disparaging is held up as a model for practice in hard times, and some practitioners bow to others as a reminder that everyone can become a Buddha.

o: a hermit who never spoke a harsh word in his life
a monk who bowed to all, saying they'd become Buddhas
a king who refused to punish anyone who insulted him

p: the Buddha, in a past life

s: the monk in this chapter taught mainly by giving long sermons
the chapter says he bowed and repeated one message to everyone he met.
the Buddha says he himself was this monk in a past life
and some of those who mocked the monk are in the assembly listening.
when people struck him, the monk stopped saying his message
he stepped back out of reach and said it again from a distance.

games.q: you have bowed to a stranger and said, 'I do not despise you; you will become a Buddha.' they pick up a stick. what do you do?
o: stop saying it; it only causes trouble
step back out of reach and say it again
games.why: the monk neither struck back nor gave up: he moved out of range and called the same words from further off, for a long time.

practice: Bring to mind, one at a time, people you're likely to see today, someone at home, someone at work, a stranger behind a counter, and for each let there be a small inward bow, as if to say: I see you.
Then bring to mind one person who is hard for you, and offer the same small bow, from as far off as you need.

wordCard.voice: Never Disparaging. In the Lotus Sutra, the monk who bowed to everyone and told them they would become Buddhas, and who, the Buddha says, was himself in a past life. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the monk's name; the Chinese translation calls him Never Disparaging.

carryVoice: Your line: I do not despise you. He never once changed his line. Until tomorrow.
